sections.model_projection: The model projects Illinois to win at home 27.36 to 24.79, a margin of 2.58 points in favor of the Illini. The projected total of 52.15 sits 1.35 points below the market total of 53.5. Illinois carries a 57.1% win probability per the model, making this a genuine toss-up despite the home team being favored. The market line of Illinois -6.0 is 3.4 points more generous to Illinois than the model's implied margin.
sections.offensive_matchup: Illinois holds a clear advantage in the passing game, ranking 8th nationally in opponent-adjusted offensive passing EPA per play (a measure of expected points added on each pass attempt, accounting for opponent quality) at 0.52, while Duke's pass defense ranks 105th at 0.35 EPA allowed per pass play — meaning Duke has been one of the more exploitable secondaries in the country. Duke's offense, on the other hand, ranks 83rd in overall offensive EPA per play at 0.16, and its 41.4% offensive success rate (the share of plays that gain enough yardage to stay on schedule) ranks 90th, suggesting the Blue Devils will struggle to sustain drives against an Illinois defense that, while not elite, is more capable than Duke's unit. The rushing matchup is essentially a wash, with both teams posting modest rushing EPA numbers and neither offensive line nor defensive front standing out dramatically in the run game.
sections.quarterback_edge: Both quarterbacks are transfer starters with similar career profiles. Illinois's Katin Houser has attempted 836 career passes at 63.0% completion and 7.7 yards per attempt across 28 games with 10-plus attempts, giving him a modest experience edge over Duke's Walker Eget, who has completed 57.4% of 698 career attempts at 7.77 yards per attempt across 19 such games. The model gives Illinois a slight edge at the position, though the gap is narrow — Eget's per-attempt production is nearly identical to Houser's, and neither has a recorded EPA per dropback on file. The edge tilts to Illinois primarily on volume of experience and the surrounding offensive infrastructure.
sections.trenches: Duke's offensive line is the clearest trench advantage in this game, ranking 19th in opponent-adjusted sack rate allowed (3.1% of dropbacks) and 22nd in havoc allowed (the share of plays disrupted by a sack, TFL, forced fumble, or turnover) at 6.9% — Duke's protection has been genuinely strong. Illinois's defensive front, however, ranks 111th in sack rate at 4.8% and 112th in havoc rate at 8.1%, meaning Duke's line should have time to operate. Flipping it around, Duke's defensive front ranks 56th in sack rate but faces an Illinois offensive line that allowed havoc on 9.4% of plays (81st), so neither pass rush is dominant. The model gives the defensive front edge to Duke (-2 edge score favoring away), reflecting that Duke's protection advantage over Illinois's pass rush is more meaningful than Illinois's front can overcome.
sections.explosive_play_edge: Illinois's defense has been exceptional at limiting explosive plays — defined as rushes of 10-plus yards or passes of 20-plus yards — allowing them on just 6.9% of opponent plays, ranking 4th nationally on an opponent-adjusted basis. Duke's offense generates explosives at a 13.0% rate (58th), so the Illini defense should be able to cap the Blue Devils' big-play ceiling. Duke's defense, by contrast, has allowed explosives at a 12.4% rate (87th), which is a vulnerability Illinois's passing attack — ranked 8th in passing EPA — can exploit. The model gives Illinois a slight edge in this category, and the interaction between Illinois's passing efficiency and Duke's leaky secondary is the most likely source of chunk plays in this game.
sections.third_down_red_zone: Duke's third-down defense is a concern, allowing opponents to convert at a 40.0% rate (91st), while Illinois converts at 43.7% (40th) — a combination that should give the Illini reasonable success extending drives. In the red zone, Illinois holds a meaningful edge: the Illini convert red-zone trips into touchdowns at a 76.4% rate (32nd) compared to Duke's defense allowing touchdowns on 59.1% of red-zone visits (53rd), and Illinois's 5.29 points per scoring opportunity ranks 4th nationally. Duke's offense, meanwhile, scores touchdowns on only 67.0% of red-zone trips (81st) and averages just 4.06 points per scoring opportunity (69th). These red-zone and scoring-efficiency gaps favor Illinois turning field position into points more reliably than Duke can.
sections.roster_talent: Illinois holds a modest talent edge, with a roster talent percentile of 70 versus Duke's 65, and a four-year blue-chip ratio of 11% compared to Duke's 8%. Both programs have very low returning production — Illinois returns 22% of total production and Duke 24%, with both teams at zero returning passing production, reflecting heavy roster turnover likely driven by the transfer portal. Illinois does return 76% of its rushing production, a meaningful continuity advantage in the run game, while Duke returns 45% of rushing production. The talent edge is real but not dramatic, and the low continuity on both sides adds uncertainty to early-season projections.
sections.recent_form: Both teams have played exactly one game, so recent form data is limited to a single-game sample and the model assigns no form-based edge to either side. Duke's raw Week 1 results show 17 points scored and 3 allowed, while Illinois scored 42 and allowed 23 in its opener. The opponent-adjusted blended metrics temper both results significantly — Duke's adjusted offense ranks 83rd and Illinois's adjusted defense ranks 93rd — suggesting the raw scores reflect opponent quality differences more than true team strength. With only one game of data, these numbers carry inherent uncertainty and should be weighted accordingly.
sections.market_movement: The spread opened at Illinois -8.5 and has moved 2.5 points toward Duke, landing at Illinois -6.0 on DraftKings. That movement crosses the key number of 7, which historically carries outsized significance in football outcomes. The total has held steady at 53.5 with no movement. The model's projected margin of 2.58 points differs from the current market spread of 6.0 by 3.4 points in Duke's favor, and there is a 0.5-point disagreement across books on the spread. Public betting percentages are unavailable, so the cause of the line movement cannot be attributed to any specific source.

sections.expected_game_script: Illinois should control the early tempo by leveraging its passing efficiency advantage — Houser operating behind a line that allowed zero sacks in Week 1 against a Duke defensive front that ranks only 56th in sack rate — to move the chains at a 43.7% third-down clip. Duke's offense will likely lean on the run early given its 35.5% raw pass rate in Week 1, but the Blue Devils' rushing EPA (99th) and line yards (86th) suggest limited upside on the ground against an Illinois defense that, while not elite, held opponents to a negative rushing EPA in Week 1. Duke's best path to staying competitive is through Walker Eget's arm, but the Blue Devils' passing EPA ranks 67th and they face an Illinois secondary that has allowed explosives on just 6.9% of plays, capping the ceiling on chunk plays. Illinois should build a modest lead in the second half as its red-zone efficiency converts drives into touchdowns at a higher rate than Duke's defense can prevent. However, Duke's strong offensive line protection should give Eget enough time to keep the Blue Devils in the game, and the model's 2.58-point projected margin suggests this stays competitive into the fourth quarter. A final score in the range of 27-24 or 28-21 fits the model's output, with Illinois winning but not covering a 6-point spread.
